Isaac Bashevis Singer. A Polish-born writer who made Yiddish—a language Jewish intellectuals were abandoning—into the vehicle for profound literary modernism. His stories and novels blend folklore, demonology, and psychological realism into a vision of Eastern European Jewish life and its American diaspora. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in nineteen seventy-eight, the only writer primarily in Yiddish ever to receive that honor.

The Magician of Lublin, published in nineteen sixty, is a picaresque novel of a con artist and seducer who gradually awakens to spiritual truth. His earlier masterpiece Satan in Goray, from nineteen thirty-five, was set amid a false Messiah's cult, blending chronicle and psychological terror. But he may be remembered most for his short stories—Gimpel the Fool and The Spinoza of Market Street are modernist masterpieces that shimmer between despair and faith.

Singer emigrated to New York in nineteen thirty-five, and his fiction bridges Eastern European shtetl and American metropolis, nostalgia and estrangement. He wrote exclusively in Yiddish and translated his own work to English, arguing passionately that Yiddish literature was living, not dead. His fiction integrates Jewish folklore, demons, spirits, and mysticism into psychological realism—blurring the line between rational and mythic modes.

He remains the sole Yiddish author to win the Nobel Prize, champion of the language's literary possibility. His stories are repositories of Eastern European folk motifs, preserving through his imagination a world destroyed in the Holocaust. Hasidic and Kabbalistic ideas infuse his psychological fiction throughout.
